classical.title: Equally likely outcomes
classical.text: For a finite sample space with equally likely outcomes, probability of A is the number of outcomes in A divided by the total number of outcomes.

axioms.title: Probability axioms
axioms.text: Probabilities are nonnegative. The whole sample space has probability one. The probability of a countable union of pairwise disjoint events is the sum of their probabilities.

complement.title: Complement rule
complement.text: The probability of not A is one minus the probability of A. The empty event has probability zero.

addition.title: Addition rule
addition.text: The probability of A or B is probability A plus probability B minus their overlap. Or is inclusive.

bounds.title: Feasible intersection
bounds.text: The overlap cannot be negative or larger than either event, and it must be large enough that their union is at most one.

conditional.title: Conditional probability
conditional.text: The probability of A given B is the probability of the overlap divided by the probability of B, provided B has positive probability.

multiply.title: Multiplication rule
multiply.text: A joint probability is a conditional probability multiplied by its conditioning probability. The relevant conditioning events must have positive probability.

chain.title: Chain rule
chain.tex: P(A\cap B\cap C)=P(A)P(B\mid A)P(C\mid A\cap B)
chain.text: For three events, multiply probability A, probability B given A, and probability C given both A and B, assuming the conditioning probabilities are defined.

total.title: Total probability
total.text: When H one through H k form a partition, total probability of B is the sum of each scenario probability times the probability of B in that scenario. Terms with zero prior probability contribute zero.

bags.title: Two-bag calculation
bags.text: Green has probability two thirds. Given green, the probability of bag A is five eighths.

independent.title: Independence
independent.text: Two events are independent exactly when their joint probability equals the product of their probabilities.

bayes.title: Bayes rule
bayes.text: The probability of the hypothesis given a positive signal equals true-positive probability divided by total positive probability, when the total is nonzero.

bayes-numbers.title: The alert example
bayes-numbers.text: With a one percent base rate, ninety percent sensitivity, and five percent false-positive rate, a positive alert has about a fifteen point three eight percent chance of being a real issue.

general-bayes.title: General Bayes rule
general-bayes.text: For a partition of hypotheses, divide a hypothesis weighted likelihood by the sum of all weighted likelihoods. The denominator must be positive.

odds.title: Odds and probability
odds.text: Odds in favor are probability divided by one minus probability. Probability is odds divided by one plus odds. The first formula requires probability below one.

odds-bayes.title: Bayes in odds form
odds-bayes.text: Posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio, when the denominators are positive.

two-tests.title: Two positive results
two-tests.text: Assuming results are independent conditional on the true state, two positive results give probability eight elevenths, or about seventy-two point seven three percent.

second-marginal.title: Updated marginal probability
second-marginal.text: After one positive, the next positive has probability twenty-two thirty-fifths. It is not the original marginal probability of zero point five six.

repeated.title: Repeated independent evidence
repeated.text: For conditionally independent results with constant sensitivity s and false-positive rate f, multiply the prior by the likelihood of m positives and n negatives in each state, then normalize.

product-count.title: Counting principle
product-count.text: Multiply the number of options at each stage when each partial choice has the stated number of continuations.

permutation.title: Ordered selection without replacement
permutation.text: The number of ordered selections of r distinct objects from n is n factorial divided by n minus r factorial.

combination.title: Unordered selection without replacement
combination.text: The number of unordered selections divides ordered selections by r factorial, removing the orders of the same selected objects.

coin-count.title: Exactly two tails
coin-count.text: For four independent fair coin tosses, choose which two positions contain tails: six equally likely sequences out of sixteen.
